job: Variable valve timing (oil control) solenoid replacement
held_reason: Second attempt, 2026-11-20. The economy class now has an example and two parts sources (2015 Toyota Corolla 1.8L: genuine list price and a new aftermarket price) but still has no labor time: no source that states a time, with a unit, for replacing one solenoid alone on an economy car was found. Subaru's 1.1 for the 2012+ Impreza includes the swap test and drive cycles and prints no unit; Mazda's 1.8 hours for the Mazda3 includes cleaning the oil pan; a community how-to's 10 minutes for a Hyundai Accent is unsigned by any professional. Midsize, truck and luxury are filled. The midsize and luxury labor time is a single Honda/Acura warranty time (0.8 hr) for the V6 rocker arm oil control (spool) valve, so their hours low and high are the same figure; the other maker times found for cam timing solenoids include diagnosis, cover two solenoids or print no unit, so they are cross-checks only.
unit: per solenoid: one variable valve timing oil control solenoid or valve fitted (the electrically operated valve that feeds oil to the variable valve timing or valve lift system; on the Honda and Acura V6 examples this is the front rocker arm oil control valve, also called the spool valve; on the Toyota example one camshaft timing oil control valve on one side). Many engines have two to four of these and each is priced separately. Not included: diagnosis, the cam phaser or actuator, timing chain work, an engine oil change, valve cover gaskets where the cover must come off, or the second solenoid

finding: The site has no live range for this job, so there is nothing to grade; these are first figures, and the file is held because the economy class still has no labor time. Built totals (part + stated hours x $120-$160/hr, the national middle labor rate used for these checks), for one solenoid: midsize 2012 Honda Accord V6 about $210-$574 and luxury 2014 Acura RDX about $210-$574 (the same Honda front spool valve, $113.95 aftermarket to $445.70 genuine list, 0.8 hr); truck 2015 Toyota Tacoma 4.0L about $248-$696 (genuine valve $152.09 discounted to $216.22 list, 0.8-3.0 hr); economy 2015 Toyota Corolla 1.8L: parts only, $59.30 (new aftermarket) to $167.98 (genuine list) for one valve, with no total built because no labor time was found. Against the benchmarks: FIXD ($170-$400) and YourMechanic ($186-$440) overlap the lower half of the built totals and RepairPal ($469-$594) sits at the upper end; nothing found falls outside roughly $170-$700. How solid the labor times are, stated plainly. Midsize and luxury rest on one manufacturer warranty time each, 0.8 hr to replace the front rocker arm oil control valve, printed in a Honda bulletin that names the 2008-12 Accord V6 and an Acura bulletin that names the 2013-15 RDX. Those are real maker times for the example vehicles, but a warranty time is the low end of what a shop bills and no second stated time was found, so the labor range for those two classes is a single point and a real quote will usually be somewhat higher. The valve on these V6 engines controls valve lift and cylinder shut-off through the rocker arms; it is Honda's version of this part, not a cam-phaser solenoid. The truck range is wide and weak: the high end is a parts seller's approximate 3-hour do-it-yourself figure for the Tacoma 4.0L, and the low end is the Honda 0.8 hr for a different maker's V6 sport utility, used because no Toyota time was found. The economy class has parts prices but no usable time: Subaru prints 1.1 for the 2012+ Impreza but that includes the swap test and drive cycles and carries no unit, Mazda's 1.8 hours for the Mazda3 includes cleaning the oil pan (1.4 hours of it), and a community how-to's 10 minutes for a Hyundai Accent is not a professional source; all are recorded as cross-checks only. Other maker figures found on this second attempt are also cross-checks, because each includes diagnosis, covers two solenoids or prints no unit: FCA 0.6 hr for both intake solenoids on the 3.6L Grand Cherokee and Durango, GM 0.7 including diagnosis for the rocker arm oil control valve on the 2014 Malibu and Impala 2.5L, Toyota 0.7-0.8 (bank 2) and 1.5-2.6 (bank 1) with no unit on its 3.5L V6 cars, Ford 1.3 hrs including reading codes for one solenoid on the 2018 F-150 5.0L, and Ford 0.7 to 3.6 hrs to diagnose and replace both solenoids on the 5.4L F-150 depending on year. Taken together they say the same thing as the ranges here: under an hour where the solenoid is on the outside of the engine, and up to three hours or more where a valve cover or intake parts must come off. Hyundai and Kia bulletins loaded for this job dealt with engine replacement, not the oil control valve, and print no time for it. General Motors bulletins for the 2.4L Equinox and Terrain and for several V6 and V8 engines name a 'Camshaft Position Actuator Solenoid Valve Replacement' operation but print 'Use Published Labor Operation Time' instead of a figure, and Nissan's bulletin refers to its flat rate manual. A parts retailer's guide reviewed by a master technician says the job runs 'anywhere from five minutes to three hours' depending on access, which fits what was found. Parts: the Corolla low end is a new Walker Products solenoid matched to the car by Toyota's part number; the Honda and Acura low end is a lesser-known aftermarket brand's new part whose page names both examples by year; the Tacoma low end is the genuine Toyota part at a dealer's discounted price, because the aftermarket parts found for it ($81-$95) were on pages that either did not say new or did not print the model year. Many engines carry two to four of these solenoids, and a shop may advise replacing a pair; these figures are for one. An estimate is not a quote and not a diagnosis.
extras: A quote often adds a diagnosis fee (the same warning light and codes can come from low or dirty oil, a clogged screen, wiring, a cam phaser or a stretched timing chain, so a shop will test before replacing the solenoid), an engine oil and filter change, a new gasket, O-ring or filter screen for the solenoid, shop supplies and sales tax. On engines with more than one solenoid a shop may quote the second one on the same bank or the matching one on the other side. If the cam phaser or actuator or the timing chain is at fault, that is a separate and much larger job.
